reasoning_traces.think:
Variational inference arises from the need to approximate complex posterior distributions in graphical models when exact inference is intractable. It exploits the conjugate duality between cumulant functions and entropies in exponential families to derive variational bounds on log-likelihoods. The core idea is minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between a tractable variational distribution q(z) and the true posterior p(z|x), leading to a lower bound on the marginal likelihood. This formulation allows for iterative optimization techniques such as coordinate ascent or gradient descent. Graphical models provide the structure to decompose high-dimensional distributions into manageable factors, making variational inference scalable. The junction tree algorithm offers a canonical way to perform exact inference in trees or graphs with bounded treewidth, but fails when treewidth increases beyond computational limits. Thus, variational methods serve as a bridge between exact inference and scalability, especially in large-scale settings where traditional sampling approaches like MCMC are inefficient.
